title: Quantum Otto engine with decoupled idle levels in a non-Hermitian XY model
abstract: We study a quantum Otto cycle in a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model with a staggered imaginary magnetic field. The energy spectrum of this system naturally decouples into a pair of working levels that depend on the external field and a pair of idle levels that are completely independent of it, thereby providing the first concrete microscopic realization of the idle-level quantum heat engine architecture proposed by de~Oliveira and Jonathan [Phys. Rev. E 104, 044133 (2021)] in a physical spin model. Tuning the non-Hermitian parameter eta_0 drives a continuous transition from a dissipative regime with negative net work and net heat absorption from the hot reservoir into a genuine heat engine mode, while simultaneously enhancing both output work and efficiency. As eta_0 increases within the stable PT-unbroken phase, the engine efficiency rises significantly, reaching a substantial fraction of the Carnot limit. This effect originates from the compression of the idle-level gap, which redistributes the level occupation weights in the hot and cold equilibrium states and thereby modulates the absorbed heat. The numerator of the net work expression is independent of eta_0, but the denominator depends on eta_0 indirectly through hyperbolic cosine functions -- this is the mathematical root of the idle-level control mechanism. We provide a detailed analysis of the robustness of these findings against parameter variations, a critical comparison of the non-Hermitian control with the Hermitian limit, and a concrete experimental proposal for trapped-ion quantum simulators. Our results demonstrate that non-Hermiticity serves as an indispensable tool for steering both the operation mode and the performance of a quantum engine.
summary: The authors analyze a quantum Otto cycle in a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model, demonstrating that the system naturally possesses decoupled 'idle levels.' By tuning the non-Hermitian parameter ($\eta_0$), they show this idle-level mechanism allows for independent control over efficiency, driving the engine into an efficient heat engine regime and confirming non-Hermiticity as a powerful tool in quantum thermodynamics.
main_problem: The study investigates a quantum Otto cycle using an idle-level heat engine architecture realized within a physical spin model to demonstrate non-Hermiticity's role in controlling thermal machine performance.
main_result: Tuning the non-Hermitian parameter ($\eta_0$) drives the system from a dissipative regime ($W<0$) into a genuine heat engine mode ($W>0$), simultaneously enhancing both output work and efficiency towards the Carnot limit.
method: The analysis employs the non-Hermitian canonical thermodynamic framework, calculating equilibrium properties using the biorthogonal eigenbasis for the four strokes of the Otto cycle.
model_or_system: The system is a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model featuring a staggered imaginary magnetic field. The Hamiltonian naturally decouples into working levels (dependent on external fields) and idle levels (independent of external fields).
key_observables: Net work ($W$), engine efficiency ($\eta = W/Q_h$), heat absorbed ($Q_h$), and the energy spectrum.
important_parameters: The non-Hermitian parameter $\eta_0$ is the primary control knob, which must be kept within the PT-unbroken phase ($|\eta_0| < 1$).
main_assumptions: The work-efficiency synergy is demonstrated for the quasistatic Otto cycle; finite-time cycles are assumed to degrade performance. The adiabatic process requires $\eta_0$ to remain away from the exceptional point ($\eta_0 = 1$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transition of net work ($W$) from negative (dissipative) to positive (engine) as $\eta_0$ increases, and show that efficiency ($\eta$) enhances monotonically with $\eta_0$. Figure 4 details how idle-level occupation differences modulate absorbed heat ($Q_h$).
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and its energy level decoupling. It then applies the non-Hermitian canonical framework to calculate thermodynamic quantities for the four strokes of the Otto cycle, culminating in demonstrating the idle-level control mechanism that enhances work and efficiency.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete realization of an advanced quantum thermodynamics concept—the idle-level engine—using non-Hermiticity as a tunable resource to surpass standard thermodynamic limitations in spin models.

figures.caption: Figure 1 shows the net work W as a function of the non-Hermitian parameter η0. For small values of η0, W < 0, and numerical veriﬁcation yields Qh > 0, Qc > 0, conﬁrming that the system operates in the dissipative regime. At a critical value ηc the net work vanishes, marking the transition point. For η0 above this critical value, W > 0 and the system enters the heat engine regime. This bidirectional behavior is a direct consequence of the idle-level mechanism [32]: changing η0 tunes the idle-level gap B = 2J p

FIG. 1. Net work W (in units of J) versus the non-Hermitian parameter η0. The horizontal dashed line marks W = 0; the vertical dashed line indicates the critical value ηc ≈0.6496, with the dissipative regime on the left and the heat engine mode on the right. The inset shows the entropy production per cycle ∆Stot in the dissipative regime, which remains positive for all η0 < ηc. Parameters: J = 1, γ = 0.3, hH = 1.5, hC = 0.8, Th = 2.0, Tc = 0.5.

Figure 4 displays the idle-level occupation diﬀerence p3 −p4 in the hot and cold equilibrium states as a function of η0, clearly revealing the microscopic origin of the eﬃciency enhancement. As η0 grows, the occupation diﬀerence on the cold side drops much faster than that on the hot side. This asymmetric change widens the occupation-diﬀerence gap that drives Qh. Therefore, the redistribution of level occupations is the physical root of the eﬃciency boost and highlights the central role of idle levels in the non-Hermitian quantum heat engine.

FIG. 2. Engine eﬃciency η versus η0. Black solid line: heat engine eﬃciency; red dashed line: Carnot limit ηC = 0.75. The eﬃciency rises from about 3.5% at η0 = 0.66 to 42.7% at η0 = 0.9, and approaches 44.15% as η0 →1−. Parameters are the same as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 3. Net work W (left axis, black solid line) and engine eﬃciency η (right axis, blue dashed line) as functions of η0. The red dashed line marks the Carnot eﬃciency ηC = 0.75. Inside the engine regime (η0 > ηc), both quantities increase with η0. Parameters are the same as in Fig. 1.
